Introduction

+

Training large language models and vision-language models usually has a fairly clear optimization story: turn text into tokens, organize most of the compute into regular Transformer blocks, and then optimize around matrix multiplication, memory access, and collective communication. A VLA (Vision-Language-Action) model is not a simple sum of a language model and an action predictor. One training iteration has to handle multi-camera video, language instructions, robot state, and continuous actions, passing in turn through a vision encoder, a language model, and an action-generation network. To a GPU this is one compute graph; to the training backend it is a complex system spanning video decoding, dynamic multimodal sequences, heterogeneous model structures, and distributed updates.

+

GR00T-N1.7 has all of these traits: it has about 3.1B parameters, and training freezes the Backbone and updates only the Action Head. This reduces backward compute but also creates an asymmetric workload: the Backbone carries the multimodal forward pass, the Action Head handles forward, backward, and parameter updates, and data processing and cross-GPU communication are spread across different phases of an iteration.

+

With a composite workload like this, no single optimization is enough. The first job is therefore to characterize how one GR00T-N1.7 iteration spends its time under the current training configuration and to identify the key bottlenecks. This post groups the optimizations into three levels and discusses how each arises and how it is implemented:

+
    +
  1. Data supply: fix duplicate video decoding, and use asynchronous shard prefetch so data processing keeps up with GPU compute;
    2. +
  2. Model compute: remove dynamic metadata, redundant outputs, and high-frequency small-kernel overhead from the frozen Backbone;
    3. +
  3. Training execution and distributed: reduce execution fragmentation with CUDA Graph, a cross-iteration pipeline, and fewer gradient memory passes.
    4. +
+

These three lines correspond to data, compute, and execution, and together raise training throughput to 1.79x that of the original implementation.

+

1. Locating the bottleneck: time goes to the frozen Backbone and fragmented execution

+

GR00T-N1.7 is a typical Vision-Language-Action architecture. Input images and text first pass through a Qwen3-VL Backbone to produce vision-language features, and an Action Head then predicts robot actions using flow matching and a 32-layer DiT. The official community training configuration freezes the Backbone and trains only the Action Head. Under the same training configuration, we measured the NVIDIA Isaac-GR00T community DDP implementation and saw abnormal throughput jitter (Figure 1).

+ +

The cause is that the Isaac data layer has no deduplication for the same episode. When one episode is split into 10 splits scattered across different shards, and there is no dedup cache, that episode can be fully decoded up to 10 times, spawning a large number of native FFmpeg threads. When many workers across many ranks consume at the same pace, they trigger decoding at the same time, and dozens of decoder threads fight the main training thread for CPU time. The main thread, which issues GPU kernel launches, is delayed by scheduling; the GPU does not receive its next instructions in time, and the result is throughput that swings up and down.

+

We broke down a single step with Nsight Systems and extracted the time share of the whole iteration:

+

Table 1: Time and share of each phase in one TrainStep

Table 1 shows that most of an iteration is spent in Forward + Backward. A closer look with the Profiler shows GPU idle gaps inside the Forward phase (Figure 2), accompanied by small kernels such as RoPE, pointwise ops, and layout/cat. Also, the Backbone's default forward still computes the large lm_head matmul every step, yet only the VLM features are needed here and the lm_head result is never used downstream, so that step is redundant.

+ +

At the kernel level, each GPU launches about 26,852 kernels per step, and about 21,005 of them (78.22% of all calls) average under 20 μs. The bottleneck is therefore not a single GEMM, but the continuous launch of a large number of fragmented kernels, plus host-side synchronization that repeatedly interrupts the GPU execution queue.

+

2. Data supply: eliminate duplicate decoding and add asynchronous prefetch

+

2.1 The duplicate episode decoding behind DataLoader jitter

+

Robot data stores its metadata per episode: an episode contains continuous video, state, and actions, while the unit of training sampling is a single step inside it. After analyzing the community implementation, we found that its shard index and the underlying dataset index have no stable mapping between them, so different samples can repeatedly hit and fully decode the same episode. Every video decode launches FFmpeg-related threads; when several DataLoader workers decode duplicates concurrently, the many decoder threads occupy CPU scheduling resources, the main training thread cannot issue kernels to the GPU in time, idle gaps appear on the GPU timeline, and step time fluctuates noticeably.

+

As Figure 3 shows, the fix is not to add more workers, but to rebuild the index relationship between training samples and their original episodes. Concretely, we first traverse all episodes and, based on the action horizon, filter out trailing steps that cannot form a complete action sequence, building a unique locator for every valid training sample. We then keep the community's existing episode grouping and shard load-balancing strategy, and when a worker consumes a shard it uses the locator to read the correct sample position. This does not change the sampling semantics or data distribution, and it avoids repeated lookups, repeated decoding of the same episode, and repeated construction of local indexes.

+ +

2.2 Hiding shard preparation with asynchronous prefetch

+

Fixing the index avoids pointless duplicate decoding, but preparing a shard still takes time. So we build upcoming shards asynchronously with a bounded thread pool: while the DataLoader consumes the current shard, the prefetch queue prepares the following shards in parallel; after a shard is consumed, the already-built result is taken from the head of the queue and a new task is added. Two design points matter for correctness and stability:

+
    +
  • Each prefetch thread holds its own shallow-copied dataset and resets the episode cache and decoder state. Otherwise several threads would share a video decoder, which easily corrupts cache consistency under concurrent reads.
    • +
  • Random transforms such as image augmentation must not draw random numbers independently in concurrent threads. Otherwise a change in thread completion order shifts the augmentation sequence under the same seed and breaks accuracy alignment.
    • +
+

So we first generate the transform replay parameters in training consumption order, and then hand the determined replay to the prefetch threads (Figure 4). The asynchronous mechanism then changes only execution timing, not random semantics.

+ +

3. Model compute: cut redundant overhead in the frozen Backbone

+

Instrumenting the Profiler for a complete GR00T-N1.7 training step showed two significant idle gaps on the GPU timeline: one between Vision Conv3D and the first Vision Block, and another between writing the visual tokens and the first Text Block (Figure 2). Neither is caused by large matrix computation; both come from metadata construction on the CPU side.

+ +

3.1 Turning per-step dynamic metadata into invariants reused by signature

+

Qwen3-VL dynamically generates several kinds of auxiliary information from image_grid_thw, including:

+
    +
  • the index and weight for position interpolation;
    • +
  • the position ids and frequency-table indices for Vision RoPE;
    • +
  • cu_seqlens and max_seqlen used by FlashAttention;
    • +
  • the positions of image tokens within the text sequence;
    • +
  • the multimodal position ids, rope delta, and token type.
    • +
+

A general-purpose implementation must support arbitrary image sizes and sequence shapes, so by default it recomputes all of this every step. In GR00T-N1.7 training, however, the image preprocessing size, spatial merge rule, and batch layout are highly stable, so rebuilding metadata for the same grid signature is redundant. In addition, .item(), .tolist(), boolean reductions, and H2D copies in that construction trigger host-device synchronization and make the main GPU compute path wait.

+

To address this we designed a two-level metadata cache (Figure 5):

+
    +
  • While the batch is still on the CPU, generate position metadata from the input content and shape, avoiding scalar readbacks after the data has moved to the GPU;
    • +
  • During CUDA Graph preparation, build Vision metadata keyed by grid_signature = ((T, H, W), ...), and bind it by the stable data_ptr() of static tensors at replay time.
    • +
+

Caching by content avoids recomputing identical inputs, and binding by pointer avoids dynamic Python lookups during Graph replay. When the grid, token count, or attention mask shape changes, the system validates the Graph contract, and a batch that cannot be safely reused does not inherit existing metadata.

+

3.2 Skipping the 151,936-dim vocabulary projection that action loss never uses

+

lm_head maps Backbone output to language vocabulary logits, but GR00T-N1.7 training uses only the hidden states to compute the action loss and never consumes language logits. The 2048 → 151936 vocabulary projection in the default forward is therefore redundant for this model. We return the Backbone hidden states directly and skip lm_head in GR00T-N1.7 training; other tasks that need language logits keep the original forward behavior.

+

3.3 Fusing RoPE and pointwise ops to cut kernel launches and intermediate tensors

+

In the Profiler, vectorized_elementwise_kernel is called 16,260 times per step, and 80 of the 98 CatArrayBatchedCopy calls come from rotate_half() in Vision/Text RoPE. A typical PyTorch implementation looks like this:

+ 
def rotate_half(x):
+    x1 = x[..., : x.shape[-1] // 2]
+    x2 = x[..., x.shape[-1] // 2 :]
+    return torch.cat((-x2, x1), dim=-1)
+
+q = q * cos + rotate_half(q) * sin
+k = k * cos + rotate_half(k) * sin
+

Mathematically this is only a rotation plus multiply-add, but at execution time it expands into slice, neg, cat, mul, and add kernels, producing intermediate tensors and layout copies. The cost in any one block is limited, but repeated across 24 Vision Blocks and 16 Text Blocks, the accumulated cost is not negligible. For this high-frequency pattern we implemented separate fused CUDA kernels for Vision RoPE and Text RoPE: one kernel reads q/k/cos/sin, completes the half rotation and multiply-add, and writes the result. We then also fused two pointwise patterns in the frozen Text Backbone (Figure 5):

+
    +
  • RMSNorm keeps its original FP32 reduction semantics and finishes normalization and weight scaling in the same kernel;
    • +
  • the SiLU(gate) * up in the MLP is merged, saving an intermediate activation tensor and one elementwise pass.
    • +
+

The fused kernels do not replace every call unconditionally. The fused path is used only when the input is a CUDA tensor, rank/shape and the cos/sin dtype satisfy the constraints, and no input requires gradients; Text Norm and MLP additionally check contiguity, dtype, device, and frozen status. If any condition fails, execution falls back to the original Transformers implementation.

+

4. Training execution: restructure iteration scheduling and distributed communication

+

Operator fusion reduces the number of execution nodes, but every step still carries a lot of Python, dispatcher, and CUDA launch overhead. Squeezing individual short kernels further has diminishing returns (Figure 6), so we need to change how the iteration executes as a whole.

+ +

4.1 Choosing a Full-Iteration CUDA Graph

+

When evaluating CUDA Graph, we did not limit the capture scope to a single module or a microbatch forward. For GR00T-N1.7, partial capture still splits the training loop into several phases: beyond the forward Graph there are backward, DDP bucket AllReduce, gradient clipping, the optimizer step, input copies, and random-number preparation. The CPU still has to schedule across those boundaries, and small kernels across phases cannot be fully frozen, so we capture the complete training iteration:

+ 
Forward
+  → action loss
+  → Backward + DDP AllReduce
+  → grad norm / clip
+  → AdamW step
+

Before capture, we run an eager warmup to materialize optimizer state and stable grad buffers; we then allocate address-stable tensors for inputs, outputs, learning rate, random numbers, and Graph results. During Graph replay no new training objects are created: we only copy the next batch into the static buffers and replay the captured CUDA work.

+

The key to this approach is not calling torch.cuda.graph(), but turning an execution path that depends on Python and dynamic shapes into a stable Graph contract:

+
    +
  • FlashAttention mask handling cannot run attention_mask.all() or max().item() during capture, so unpadding metadata is cached ahead of time;
    • +
  • image grid, token count, attention mask, and sequence length must be validated before replay;
    • +
  • flow-matching timesteps sampled on the CPU are moved through a pinned host buffer and a dedicated stream, preserving the original random-number consumption order;
    • +
  • the CUDA generator state is registered with the Graph to keep replay semantics for dropout and action noise;
    • +
  • DDP AllReduce stays inside the Graph, avoiding repeated synchronization outside capture.
    • +
+

4.2 Using the frozen boundary for a cross-iteration Backbone forward

+

The Full Graph reduces launch fragmentation, but NCCL communication at the tail of backward still cannot be fully hidden. The frozen structure of GR00T-N1.7 offers a further opening: the Backbone forward of batch n+1 does not depend on the optimizer update of batch n.

+

So we further split the full execution graph into two Graphs:

+
    +
  1. Backbone Graph: runs only the frozen Qwen3-VL forward and writes the result into a separate staging buffer;
    2. +
  2. Train Graph: reads the stable Backbone output and runs the Action Head forward, backward, DDP communication, gradient handling, and the optimizer.
    3. +
+

In steady state, while the Train Graph is processing batch n, a dedicated Backbone stream has already started on batch n+1. Once the Backbone output is ready, a producer-consumer dependency is established through an event, and the output is copied into the Train Graph's static input. Meanwhile, the copy stream keeps prefetching batch n+2.

+

This does not run the forward and backward of the same batch in parallel, because they have a real data dependency. What it exploits is the dependency-free window between different batches, and the frozen boundary guarantees that parameters cannot go out of version between the two pipelines. Before running, we also check that requires_grad=False holds for every Backbone parameter; once the Backbone participates in training, this pipeline assumption no longer holds. The scheme not only computes part of the next batch's forward early, it also uses that compute to cover part of the exposed NCCL communication of the current batch.

+

4.3 Covering exposed communication and reducing repeated gradient memory access

+

After the cross-iteration Backbone pipeline covers part of the communication, the next focus is the memory reads and writes after backward. On the traditional path, the same gradient goes through at least three kinds of extra operations:

+
    +
  • before each replay, the leaf grad buffer is zeroed;
    • +
  • Autograd's AccumulateGrad performs one more grad += new_grad;
    • +
  • clip_grad_norm_ uses a separate _foreach_mul_ to write the clipping coefficient back to every gradient, and AdamW then reads it all again.
    • +
+

For a Full Graph with stable addresses and only one microbatch per step, these memory operations can be merged. Before capture, we materialize stable grad buffers for all trainable parameters; during capture/replay, backward writes the current gradients directly, avoiding "write 0, then add". Gradient clipping now computes only the global norm and a device-side scale, and no longer writes scaled gradients back separately. As Figure 7 shows, our capturable AdamW applies grad × scale the first time it reads the gradient and directly updates the first moment, second moment, and parameters.

前言

+

大语言模型和视觉语言模型的训练通常具有相对清晰的优化主线：将文本转换为 token，将主要计算组织为规则的 Transformer block，再围绕矩阵乘、显存访问和集合通信进行优化。但 VLA（Vision-Language-Action）并非语言模型与动作预测模块的简单组合，一次训练迭代需要同时处理多路相机视频、语言指令、机器人状态和连续动作，并依次经过视觉编码器、语言模型与动作生成网络。对 GPU 而言，这是一张计算图；但对训练后端而言，则是一套横跨视频解码、动态多模态序列、异构模型结构和分布式更新的复杂系统。

+

GR00T-N1.7 具备上述典型特征：模型规模约为 3.1B，训练时冻结 Backbone，仅更新 Action Head。该策略减少了反向计算，但也形成了不对称负载——Backbone 承担多模态前向，Action Head 负责前反向与参数更新，数据处理和跨卡通信则分布于训练迭代的不同阶段。

+

面对这种复合负载，单一优化手段难以达到理想效果。因此，优化工作的首要任务是准确刻画当前训练配置下 GR00T-N1.7 单次迭代的时间分布，并识别影响训练效率的关键瓶颈。本文将相关优化归纳为三个层面，并分别讨论其形成机制与实现路径：

+
    +
  1. 数据供给优化：修复重复视频解码，并通过 shard 异步预取使数据处理与 GPU 计算稳定衔接；
    2. +
  2. 模型计算优化：消除冻结 Backbone 中的动态 metadata、冗余输出和高频小算子开销；
    3. +
  3. 训练执行与分布式优化：通过 CUDA Graph、跨迭代流水与梯度访存优化减少执行碎片。
    4. +
+

这三条主线分别对应数据、计算、执行三个层面，最终将训练吞吐提升至原始实现的 1.79 倍。

+

1. 瓶颈定位：训练耗时集中于冻结 Backbone 与碎片化执行

+

GR00T-N1.7 是典型的 Vision-Language-Action 结构。输入图像和文本先经过 Qwen3-VL Backbone，得到视觉—语言特征，随后 Action Head 使用 flow matching 与 32 层 DiT 预测机器人动作。官方社区训练配置冻结 Backbone，只训练 Action Head。在保持训练配置相同的口径下，我们测得 NVIDIA Isaac-GR00T 社区 DDP 实现的训练吞吐存在异常抖动（如图 1）。

+ +

该现象源于 Isaac 数据层对同一条 episode 缺乏去重机制：当一条 episode 被切分为 10 个 split 并分散至不同 shard 时，由于没有去重缓存，该 episode 会被完整解码最多 10 次，进而产生大量 FFmpeg 原生线程。当多个 rank 的多个 worker 消费节奏一致时，会同时触发解码，导致数十个解码线程与训练主线程争抢 CPU 时间片。这使负责发起 GPU kernel launch 的训练主线程遭受调度延迟，GPU 侧无法及时收到下一批指令，最终表现为吞吐量的忽高忽低。

+

+

2. 数据供给优化：消除重复解码并建立异步预取

+

2.1 DataLoader 抖动背后的 episode 重复解码问题

+

机器人数据以 episode 为单位存储元数据：一个 episode 包含连续视频、状态和动作，而训练采样的单位是其中某个 step。分析社区实现后发现，其分片索引与底层数据集索引之间缺少稳定的对应关系，导致不同采样项可能反复命中并完整解码同一 episode。每次视频解码都会启动 FFmpeg 相关线程；当多个 DataLoader worker 并发执行重复解码时，大量解码线程占用 CPU 调度资源，导致训练主线程无法及时向 GPU 下发 kernel，最终在 GPU 时间线上形成空闲区间，并造成 step time 明显波动。

+

如图 3 所示，优化重点并非继续增加 worker 数量，而是重新建立训练样本与原始 episode 之间的索引关系。具体而言，首先遍历全部 episode，并依据 action horizon 过滤末尾无法构成完整动作序列的 step，为每个有效训练样本建立唯一定位信息；随后沿用社区已有的 episode 分组与 shard 负载均衡策略，在 worker 消费 shard 时通过该定位信息读取正确的样本位置。该方案不改变原有采样语义和数据分布，同时避免重复查找、解码同一 episode 以及重复构造局部索引。

+ +

2.2 通过异步预取隐藏后续 shard 的准备开销

+

索引修复避免了无意义的重复解码，但 shard 的准备本身仍然需要时间。为此，我们使用有界线程池异步构造后续 shard：当前 shard 被 DataLoader 消费时，预取队列并行准备后面的 shard；消费完成后，从队首取得已经构造好的结果，再补入一个新任务。这一机制包含两个影响正确性与稳定性的关键设计：

+
    +
  • 每个预取线程持有独立的浅拷贝 dataset，并重置 episode cache 与 decoder 状态。否则多个线程共享视频 decoder，容易在并发读取时破坏缓存一致性。
    • +
  • 图像增强等随机变换不能由并发线程独立生成随机数。否则，线程完成顺序的变化会导致同一 seed 下的数据增强序列发生偏移，进而破坏精度对齐。
    • +
+

为此，我们先按训练消费顺序生成 transform replay 参数，再将确定的 replay 交由预取线程执行（如图 4）。这样，异步机制仅改变执行时序，不改变随机语义。

+ +

3. 模型计算优化：减少冻结 Backbone 的冗余开销

+

通过插桩观察 GR00T-N1.7 完整训练 step 的 Profiler，发现 GPU 时间线上存在两段显著的空闲区间：一段位于 Vision Conv3D 与第一个 Vision Block 之间，另一段位于视觉 token 写入与第一个 Text Block 之间（如图 2 所示）。这两段空闲区间并非由大规模矩阵计算引起，而是源于 CPU 侧的 metadata 构造。

+ +

3.1 把每步动态 metadata 变成按签名复用的不变量

+

Qwen3-VL 需要根据 image_grid_thw 动态生成多类辅助信息，包括：

+
    +
  • 位置插值的 index 与 weight；
    • +
  • Vision RoPE 的 position id 和频率表索引；
    • +
  • FlashAttention 使用的 cu_seqlens 与 max_seqlen；
    • +
  • 图像 token 在文本序列中的位置；
    • +
  • multimodal position id、rope delta 和 token type。
    • +
+

通用实现需要支持任意图像尺寸和序列形状，因此默认在每个 step 重新计算相关信息。但 GR00T-N1.7 训练中的图像预处理尺寸、spatial merge 规则和 batch 布局高度稳定，对相同 grid signature 重复构造 metadata 属于冗余操作。同时，构造过程中的 .item()、.tolist()、布尔归约和 H2D copy 会触发 host-device 同步，造成 GPU 主计算路径等待。

+

针对上述问题，我们设计了两级 metadata 缓存（如图 5）：

+
    +
  • 在 batch 仍位于 CPU 时，按输入内容与 shape 生成 position metadata，避免数据搬上 GPU 后再做标量回读；
    • +
  • 在 CUDA Graph 准备阶段，按 grid_signature = ((T, H, W), ...) 构造 Vision metadata，并在 replay 时按静态张量的稳定 data_ptr() 绑定。
    • +
+

按内容建立缓存可避免相同输入的重复计算，按指针绑定则可避免 Graph replay 期间执行 Python 动态查找。当 grid、token 数或 attention mask 形状发生变化时，系统会校验 Graph 合约，无法安全复用的 batch 不会沿用已有 metadata。

+

3.2 跳过 action loss 未使用的 151,936 维词表投影

+

lm_head 用于将 Backbone 输出映射为语言词表 logits，而 GR00T-N1.7 训练只使用 hidden states 计算 action loss，并不消费语言 logits。因此，默认 forward 中的 2048 → 151936 词表投影对该模型属于冗余计算。针对这一冗余路径，我们在 GR00T-N1.7 训练中直接返回 Backbone hidden states 并跳过 lm_head；其他需要语言 logits 的任务仍保持原有 forward 行为。

+

3.3 融合 RoPE 与 Pointwise 计算，减少 Kernel 发射与中间张量

+

Profiler 中 vectorized_elementwise_kernel 每步调用 16,260 次；98 次 CatArrayBatchedCopy 里有 80 次来自 Vision/Text RoPE 的 rotate_half()。典型 PyTorch 实现如下：

+ 
def rotate_half(x):
+    x1 = x[..., : x.shape[-1] // 2]
+    x2 = x[..., x.shape[-1] // 2 :]
+    return torch.cat((-x2, x1), dim=-1)
+
+q = q * cos + rotate_half(q) * sin
+k = k * cos + rotate_half(k) * sin
+

该计算在数学上仅包含旋转与乘加，执行时却会展开为 slice、neg、cat、mul、add 等多个 kernel，并产生中间张量和 layout copy。单个 block 中的开销有限，但在 24 层 Vision Block 和 16 层 Text Block 中重复执行后，其累计成本不可忽略。针对这种高频模式，我们为 Vision RoPE 与 Text RoPE 分别实现了 CUDA 融合 kernel，在一次 kernel 中读取 q/k/cos/sin，直接完成 half rotation 和乘加并写出结果。随后，我们又把冻结 Text Backbone 中的两类 pointwise 模式纳入融合（如图 5 所示）：

+
    +
  • RMSNorm 保留原有 FP32 reduction 语义，在同一 kernel 内完成归一化收尾与权重缩放；
    • +
  • 合并 MLP 中的 SiLU(gate) * up，减少激活中间张量及一次逐元素遍历。
    • +
+

融合 kernel 不会无条件替换所有调用：当输入为 CUDA tensor，rank/shape 与 cos/sin dtype 均满足约束，且所有输入均不需要梯度时，才启用 fused path；Text Norm 和 MLP 同样需要校验连续性、dtype、device 与冻结状态。任一条件不满足时，均回退至 Transformers 原始实现。

+

4. 训练执行优化：重构迭代调度与分布式通信

+

算子融合减少了执行节点，但每个 step 仍包含大量 Python、dispatcher 和 CUDA launch 开销。继续优化单个耗时较短的算子，边际收益已经有限（如图 6 所示），此时需要从整体上调整迭代的执行方式。

+ +

4.1 选择 Full-Iteration CUDA Graph

+

在评估 CUDA Graph 时，我们没有将捕获范围限定在单个模块或 microbatch forward。对 GR00T-N1.7 而言，局部捕获仍会将训练循环划分为多个阶段：forward Graph 之外还包括 backward、DDP bucket AllReduce、梯度裁剪、optimizer step、输入复制和随机数准备。CPU 仍需在这些边界之间进行调度，跨阶段的小 kernel 也无法被完整固化，因此我们选择捕获完整训练迭代：

+ 
Forward
+  → action loss
+  → Backward + DDP AllReduce
+  → grad norm / clip
+  → AdamW step
+

在 capture 前，我们先完成 Eager warmup，物化优化器状态和稳定 grad buffer；随后为输入、输出、学习率、随机数与 Graph 结果分配地址稳定的 tensor。Graph replay 期间不再创建新的训练对象，只把下一批数据复制进静态 buffer，然后重放已经捕获的 CUDA 工作。

+

该方案的关键不在于调用 torch.cuda.graph()，而在于将原本依赖 Python 和动态 shape 的执行路径转化为稳定的 Graph 合约：

+
    +
  • FlashAttention mask 处理不能在 capture 中执行 attention_mask.all() 或 max().item()，因此提前缓存 unpadding metadata；
    • +
  • 图像 grid、token 数、attention mask 和序列长度必须在 replay 前验证；
    • +
  • CPU 上采样的 flow-matching timestep 通过 pinned host buffer 和独立 stream 搬运，保持原随机数消费顺序；
    • +
  • CUDA generator 状态注册到 Graph，确保 dropout 与 action noise 的 replay 语义；
    • +
  • DDP AllReduce 留在 Graph 内，避免 capture 外重复同步。
    • +
+

4.2 利用冻结边界实现跨迭代 Backbone 前向

+

Full Graph 降低了 launch 碎片化，但反向末端仍存在难以完全隐藏的 NCCL 通信。GR00T-N1.7 的冻结结构提供了进一步优化的条件：batch n+1 的 Backbone 前向不依赖 batch n 的 optimizer 更新。

+

因此，我们进一步将完整执行图拆分为两个 Graph：

+
    +
  1. Backbone Graph：只执行冻结 Qwen3-VL 前向，结果写入独立 staging buffer；
    2. +
  2. Train Graph：读取稳定的 Backbone 输出，执行 Action Head forward、backward、DDP 通信、梯度处理和 optimizer。
    3. +
+

在稳态流水中，Train Graph 正在处理 batch n 时，专用 Backbone stream 已经开始计算 batch n+1。Backbone 输出完成后，通过 event 建立生产者—消费者依赖，再拷贝到 Train Graph 的静态输入。与此同时，copy stream 继续预取 batch n+2。

+

该方案并未并行执行同一 batch 的前向与反向，因为二者存在真实的数据依赖。实际利用的是不同 batch 之间的无依赖区间，并通过冻结边界确保参数在两条流水之间不会发生版本错位。运行前还会检查 Backbone 所有参数的 requires_grad=False；一旦 Backbone 参与训练，该流水假设便不再成立。该方案不仅提前完成下一批的部分前向计算，也利用这段计算覆盖当前批次的一部分暴露 NCCL 通信。

+

4.3 覆盖暴露通信并减少梯度重复访存

+

在利用跨迭代 Backbone 流水覆盖部分通信后，进一步的优化重点转向 backward 之后的显存读写。传统路径中，同一份 gradient 至少经历三类额外操作：

+
    +
  • 每次 replay 前，把 leaf grad buffer 清零；
    • +
  • Autograd 的 AccumulateGrad 再执行一次 grad += new_grad；
    • +
  • clip_grad_norm_ 用独立的 _foreach_mul_ 把裁剪系数写回全部 gradient，随后 AdamW 又完整读取一次。
    • +
+

对于地址稳定且每次仅包含一个 microbatch 的 Full Graph，上述内存操作可以进一步合并。我们在 capture 前物化所有 trainable parameter 的稳定 grad buffer；capture/replay 时由 backward 直接写入本轮梯度，避免"先写 0、再执行 add"。同时，梯度裁剪仅计算 global norm 与 device-side scale，不再单独写回缩放后的梯度。如图 7 所示，我们实现的 capturable AdamW 在首次读取 gradient 时完成 grad × scale，并直接更新一阶动量、二阶动量与参数。

+ +

Accelerating LingBot-VA Training: A Technical Walkthrough

+
2026-10-15 · The LoongForge Team
+
+ +
+
+
GitHubhttps://github.com/baidu-baige/LoongForge
+
+

LingBot-VA is an embodied-AI model that jointly models video and action. Its training suffers from redundant parameter communication, unbalanced load from variable-length samples, per-layer chains of small kernels that slow the backward pass, and GPUs that frequently wait on CPU scheduling. LoongForge applies system-level optimization across the whole training path and achieves 2.20x training throughput and a 54.5% shorter step time.

+

1. Background: new training challenges from joint video-action modeling

+

In embodied AI, models that jointly model a "video-generation backbone + action branch" (WAM-style models) are quickly becoming mainstream. Instead of simply chaining a vision encoder and an action head, they predict both how the scene will evolve and how the robot should act, grounding control in an understanding of physical dynamics. This markedly improves long-horizon task success and sample efficiency. LingBot-VA is a representative example: it uses a large pretrained video diffusion model as its backbone, interleaves video latents and action tokens into one unified sequence, and performs autoregressive flow-matching generation. It reports leading success rates on simulation benchmarks such as RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO.

+

But this architecture puts very different pressure on the training system than a conventional VLA does:

+
    +
  • Sequences are inherently variable in length. The number of video latent frames and the length of the action chunk vary per sample, so token counts within one batch can differ by several times. With multi-GPU data parallelism, each step takes as long as the slowest GPU.
    • +
  • Per-layer small kernels are dense. In each of the 30 Transformer blocks, a chain of lightweight operations runs: time modulation, QK normalization, rotary position embedding, and residual gating. Each kernel is short, but multiplied by the layer count and the number of gradient-accumulation microbatches, kernel launches and intermediate-tensor traffic alone consume a lot of time.
    • +
  • Gradient accumulation amplifies communication. To build a large effective batch under limited memory, this kind of training commonly uses many gradient-accumulation steps. Under parameter sharding (FSDP), the default implementation all-gathers the parameters again for every microbatch, so communication volume scales directly with the number of microbatches.
    • +
  • Attention is sparse and masked. Once video tokens and action tokens are interleaved, attention needs masks built from chunks and sliding windows. Building them is a CPU-heavy graph-structured computation and easily becomes a host-side bottleneck.
    • +
+

The net effect: when training with the community open-source implementation, the GPU spends a large share of its time not computing but waiting for communication, waiting for masks, and waiting for the slowest GPU.

+

2. Overview: start from "what is the GPU waiting for?"

+

To improve LingBot-VA training efficiency, the Baidu Baige team restructured its training path at the system level on LoongForge, our open-source omni-modal training framework. We did not start by "swapping in a faster kernel". We started by using profiling to answer one question: where does the time in a step actually go?

+

Based on NSys timelines and NVTX ranges, we split step time into three kinds of waste that can be optimized independently:

+
    +
  • Communication waste: the same parameters are all-gathered repeatedly within one step, and gradient reduction uses needlessly high precision.
    • +
  • Scheduling waste: many visible launch gaps appear between GPU kernels, where the GPU waits for Python-side mask construction, for automatic garbage collection, and for the loss to be synchronized back to the host.
    • +
  • Operator waste: per-layer chains of small kernels produce many kernel launches and dtype/layout round trips, and the backward pass has to materialize extra intermediate tensors.
    • +
+

On top of these comes a load problem tied directly to the model: rank stragglers caused by variable-length samples.

+

Along these four directions, with the same model structure, data, and hyperparameters, LoongForge raises training throughput to 2.20x that of the community open-source implementation. The key techniques behind this follow.

+

3. Under the hood: four engineering optimizations behind the 2.2x

+

Optimization 1: FSDP parameter communication — from one all-gather per microbatch to one per step

+

The default semantics of sharded-parameter training are: all-gather the full parameters before forward, reshard immediately after use to free memory, and all-gather again for backward. This is reasonable with a single microbatch, but it degrades under gradient accumulation: every microbatch in a step repeats "all-gather → compute → reshard", even though all of them use exactly the same parameters.

+

LoongForge postpones resharding from "after every forward/backward" to "after the optimizer update". When wrapping with FSDP, we turn off reshard_after_forward so the parameters stay unsharded for the whole step and are reused by every microbatch. We also register a step post-hook on the optimizer so that, once the parameter update is done, everything is resharded in one go and the memory is returned. The number of parameter all-gathers per step drops from "number of microbatches × 2 (one each for forward and backward)" to 1.

+ +

An ablation quantifies this item: turning the optimization off increases step time by 21.16%. It also explains why the gain scales linearly with the number of gradient-accumulation steps: the more steps, the more repeated communication is saved.

+

A companion change concerns gradient-reduction precision. We align reduce_dtype in the FSDP mixed-precision policy with the parameter precision (BF16), which removes the precision conversions around reduce-scatter and the larger communication payload. This alone is worth about 2%, and it matches the community implementation exactly under the accuracy gate.

+

Optimization 2: load balancing for variable-length samples — cost-balanced sampling and microbatch alignment

+

Sample lengths in embodied data are naturally uneven. The default distributed sampler slices samples to ranks in index order, so some ranks get a batch of long samples and others a batch of short ones. Because gradient synchronization is a global barrier, each step takes as long as the slowest rank, and all the time saved by the short-sample ranks turns into idle waiting.

+

LoongForge implements a cost-balanced distributed sampler:

+
    +
  • The gradient-accumulation step count is used as the grouping unit, so the balancing granularity exactly covers all the samples consumed by one parameter update;
    • +
  • Within a group, samples are sorted by cost (estimated from sequence length and similar factors) in descending order and then placed greedily on the rank with the lowest accumulated cost, making the total cost of each rank as close as possible;
    • +
  • After assignment, the microbatch order inside each rank is cost-aligned, so that at the same microbatch index every rank processes samples of a similar magnitude. This avoids per-microbatch jitter where some GPUs are on long samples while others are on short ones at the same moment.
    • +
+ +

The effect is again verified with end-to-end time: with cost-balanced sampling on, step time drops by 7.4% (a 1.079x speedup). This gain changes no operator implementation and comes purely from data orchestration, which is exactly the part that operator-only optimization cannot reach.

+

Note that balancing changes the sample-to-rank mapping, so we must prove that it does not change training semantics. For this we built a SHA256 gate on sample order: we export the actual sampling order of every rank in every epoch and check it file by file against an archived baseline; if any single file differs, the gate fails.

+

Optimization 3: per-layer kernel-chain fusion — hand-written Triton RoPE, fused QK RMSNorm, compiled modulation prologue

+

The "small operations" inside the 30 blocks are the easiest cost to overlook. Each takes only a few microseconds, but it runs in every layer, for every microbatch, and leaves a trail of intermediate tensors in backward. LoongForge does three things here:

+

A hand-written Triton RoPE kernel. In eager mode, rotary position embedding expands into a chain of mul / add / cat / copy kernels, once for Q and once for K. We use a single Triton kernel to rotate Q and K pairwise at the same time, and we implement the backward ourselves: the backward rotation shares the same kernel as the forward and just negates the rotation direction, so no extra intermediate tensors need to be saved and the operator chain does not have to be rebuilt in backward. The cos/sin components are cached by shape and reused. In the ablation, turning this group off raises total elementwise time to 1.76x, adds about 5,100 kernels per step, and increases step time by 7.29%. About 98% of the gain comes from backward, which is exactly where writing our own backward pays off.

+

A fused QK RMSNorm. If Q/K normalization uses the framework's native implementation, it adds extra contiguous copies and dtype conversions before and after attention. We switch to TransformerEngine's fused RMSNorm. In the ablation, turning it off increases end-to-end step time by 6.46%, which confirms its value.

+

A compiled per-layer modulation prologue with a fixed BF16 compute domain. The per-layer time modulation (shift / scale / gate) plus LayerNorm is a typical memory-bound short chain. We treat it as one compilation unit so the compiler performs modulation and normalization in a single kernel, and we keep the intermediate expressions inside the block in BF16 with no up- and down-casting. Turning off the compiled prologue increases step time by 7.78% and raises total elementwise time to 1.9x; fixing the BF16 compute domain adds a further gain of about 1.4%.

+ +

Optimization 4: rescuing the GPU from "waiting for the host" — mask compilation and GC suppression

+

The first three items all reduce the work the GPU has to do. But profiling exposed another kind of waste: the GPU has work to do and yet sits idle waiting for the host.

+

The criterion is three structural NSys metrics: the share of GPU busy time, GPU idle time, and the total length of the "visible gaps of at least 10 microseconds" between kernels. If a change leaves the kernel count and per-category kernel time almost unchanged, but idle time and large gaps rise significantly together, it is a host-side bottleneck. Such a bottleneck cannot be fixed by optimizing operators; the host-side computation has to be moved off the critical path.

+ +

Using this criterion, we mainly located and fixed two kinds of host-side bottleneck:

+
    +
  • Attention mask construction. The sparse attention over the interleaved sequence needs a block mask built at every step, which is a Python-side graph-structured computation. Without compilation it directly blocks forward kernel submission: GPU busy falls from 99.0% to 94.8%, GPU idle grows to 5.6x, and gaps of at least 10 microseconds grow to 10.4x. Moreover, the increase in idle time almost exactly equals the increase in large gaps, millisecond for millisecond, which is the textbook signature of a GPU waiting on the host. We compile the mask construction and cache it by shape and window parameters (falling back to eager automatically if compilation fails, for robustness), taking this host computation off the critical path for a per-step gain of 3.89%.
    • +
  • Python automatic garbage collection. The training loop creates many short-lived objects. Once Python's generation-2 full GC triggers, the host has a window in which it cannot submit CUDA work. Worse, the trigger times differ across ranks, so the window is amplified through collective communication. Our strategy is not to simply disable GC: we keep the generation-0/1 young-generation collections, suppress the generation-2 threshold, and explicitly trigger one controlled full GC at a fixed step interval. The ablation shows that when this strategy is reverted, the kernel count is exactly unchanged (identical kernel by kernel), yet GPU idle grows to 2.4x and step time increases by 1.98%. The GPU compute graph is exactly the same, so the loss comes purely from host stalls.
    • +
+

4. Measured performance

+

We tested LingBot-VA with default training parameters (gradient accumulation = 10) on the LIBERO dataset, on Baidu Baige hpas.lgn7ib instances. With identical model structure, data, and hyperparameters, LoongForge achieves 2.20x the training throughput of the community open-source implementation and a 54.5% shorter step time, while the training loss stays aligned with the community implementation (mean relative error 0.171%).

+ +

From the perspective of optimization mechanisms, the size of each contribution is also clear:

+
    +
  • Amplified communication count is the only mechanism that yields a single-item gain above 20%, and the gain scales linearly with the number of gradient-accumulation steps;
    • +
  • Per-layer kernel-chain fusion (modulation prologue, Triton RoPE, fused QK RMSNorm) is worth 6%–8% each;
    • +
  • Cost-balanced sampling for variable-length samples contributes about 8% and does not depend on any operator change;
    • +
  • Host-side idle cleanup (mask compilation, GC strategy) totals about 6% and pushes GPU busy to 99.0%.
    • +
+

It is worth noting that once GPU busy reaches 99.0%, there is less than 1% left to gain on the host side. Further speedups must come from the kernels themselves (GEMM currently accounts for about 63.7% of kernel time) and from communication overlap. That is the direction of our next stage.

+

5. Summary: turning the GPU from "passively waiting" into "continuously computing"

+

Looking back over the whole effort, the 2.20x improvement comes from four paths of different nature: redesigning communication semantics (parameters reused within a step), load balancing through data orchestration (cost alignment of variable-length samples), hand-written and fused operators (Triton RoPE and per-layer chain fusion), and cleaning up the host-side critical path (mask compilation and the GC strategy). They address four kinds of waste, namely communication, load, compute, and scheduling, and dropping any one of them forfeits part of the gain.

+

What supports these conclusions is a methodology of "quantify the bottleneck first, design the optimization next, and accept it by ablation last": every conclusion comes from reproducible timeline evidence and item-by-item ablation, and every performance gain passes an accuracy gate that is aligned with the community implementation iteration by iteration.

+

All of these optimizations are now integrated into LoongForge, our omni-modal training framework. We welcome researchers and developers in embodied AI to explore more efficient VLA training together.

LingBot-VA 训练加速技术解析

+
2026-10-15 · LoongForge 团队
+
+ +
+
+
GitHubhttps://github.com/baidu-baige/LoongForge
+
+

LingBot-VA 是视频-动作联合建模的具身智能模型，其训练存在参数通信冗余、变长样本负载不均、逐层小算子链拖慢反向、GPU 频繁等待 CPU 调度等问题。LoongForge 对其完成全链路系统级优化，最终实现 2.20 倍训练吞吐提升，单步训练耗时缩短 54.5%。

+

1. 背景：视频-动作联合建模带来的训练新挑战

+

在具身智能的技术路线中，以「视频生成主干 + 动作分支」联合建模的 WAM 类模型正在快速成为主流。它们不再把视觉编码器与动作头简单串联，而是让模型同时预测「场景会怎样演化」和「机器人该怎样动作」，把控制建立在对物理动态的理解之上，从而显著提升长程任务的成功率与样本效率。LingBot-VA 正是这一路线的代表：它以大规模预训练视频扩散模型为主干，将视频 latent 与动作 token 交织成一条统一序列做自回归式的流匹配生成，在 RoboTwin 2.0 与 LIBERO 等仿真基准上都取得了领先的成功率。

+

但这种架构给训练系统带来的压力，与常规 VLA 截然不同：

+
    +
  • 序列天然变长。视频 latent 的帧数、动作 chunk 的长度随样本变化，同一个 batch 内不同样本的 token 数可以相差数倍。在多卡数据并行下，每个 step 的耗时由最慢的那张卡决定。
    • +
  • 逐层小算子密集。30 层 Transformer block 中，每层都要做时间调制（modulation）、QK 归一化、旋转位置编码、残差门控等一连串轻量操作。单个算子耗时很短，但乘上层数与梯度累积的 microbatch 数后，仅 kernel 启动与中间张量搬运就能吃掉可观的时间。
    • +
  • 通信被梯度累积放大。为了在有限显存下堆起有效批次，这类训练普遍使用较大的梯度累积步数（gradient accumulation）。在参数分片（FSDP）下，默认实现每个 microbatch 都要重新 all-gather 一遍参数，通信量被 microbatch 数直接放大。
    • +
  • 注意力是稀疏且带掩码的。视频 token 与动作 token 交织后，注意力需要按 chunk 与滑动窗口构造掩码，掩码构造本身是 CPU 密集的图结构计算，极易成为主机侧瓶颈。
    • +
+

这些特征叠加的结果是：直接用社区开源实现训练，GPU 有大量时间不在算，而在等通信、等掩码、等最慢的那张卡。

+

2. 方案概览：从「GPU 在等什么」出发

+

为提升 LingBot-VA 的训练效率，百度百舸团队基于自研开源的全模态训练框架 LoongForge，对其训练链路做了系统级重构。我们没有从「换个更快的算子」开始，而是先用 profiling 回答一个问题：一个 step 的时间，到底花在哪里。

+

基于 NSys 时间线与 NVTX 分段，我们把 step 时间拆成三类可独立优化的浪费：

+
    +
  • 通信浪费：同一份参数在一个 step 内被反复 all-gather；梯度归约使用了不必要的高精度。
    • +
  • 调度浪费：GPU kernel 之间存在大量可见空隙（launch gap），GPU 在等 Python 侧构造掩码、等自动垃圾回收、等 loss 同步回主机。
    • +
  • 算子浪费：逐层的小算子链产生大量 kernel 启动与 dtype/layout 往返，反向传播中还要额外物化中间张量。
    • +
+

再叠加一项与模型特性直接相关的负载问题——变长样本导致的 rank 掉队。

+

围绕这四个方向，LoongForge 最终在同样的模型结构、同样的数据与同样的超参下，把训练吞吐提升到社区开源实现的 2.20 倍。下面拆解这背后的关键技术实现。

+

3. 核心揭秘：2.2 倍加速背后的四大工程优化

+

优化一：FSDP 参数通信 —— 让 all-gather 从「每 microbatch 一次」降到「每 step 一次」

+

参数分片训练的默认语义是：forward 前 all-gather 出完整参数，用完立刻 reshard 释放显存；backward 再 all-gather 一次。这个语义在单 microbatch 场景下是合理的，但在梯度累积场景下会退化——一个 step 内的每个 microbatch 都会重复一遍「all-gather → 计算 → reshard」，而这些 microbatch 用的其实是完全相同的参数。

+

LoongForge 的做法是把 reshard 的时机从「每次 forward/backward 之后」推迟到「optimizer 更新之后」：在 FSDP 包装时关闭 reshard_after_forward，让参数在整个 step 内保持 unsharded 状态，多个 microbatch 直接复用；同时在优化器上注册 step post-hook，在参数更新完成后再统一 reshard，把显存归还。这样一个 step 内的参数 all-gather 次数从「microbatch 数 × 2（前反向各一次）」压缩到 1 次。

+ +

消融实验可以量化这一项的价值：把该优化关掉，单步耗时上涨 21.16%。这也解释了为什么这项优化的收益会随梯度累积步数线性放大：累积步数越大，被省掉的重复通信越多。

+

配套的一项是梯度归约精度：我们把 FSDP 混合精度策略中的 reduce_dtype 对齐到参数精度（BF16），省掉 reduce-scatter 前后的精度转换与更大的通信载荷。这一项单独约 2% 的收益，且在精度门禁下与社区实现完全对齐。

+

优化二：变长样本负载均衡 —— 代价均衡采样与 microbatch 对齐

+

具身数据的样本长度天然不齐。默认的分布式采样器按索引顺序把样本切给各个 rank，于是某些 rank 分到一批长样本、某些分到一批短样本。由于梯度同步是全局屏障，每个 step 的实际耗时等于最慢 rank 的耗时，短样本 rank 省下的时间全部变成空等。

+

LoongForge 实现了代价均衡的分布式采样器：

+
    +
  • 以梯度累积步数为一个分组单位，保证均衡的粒度正好覆盖一次参数更新所消耗的全部样本；
    • +
  • 组内先按样本代价（由序列长度等因素估计）降序排列，再用贪心策略依次投放到当前累计代价最小的 rank，使各 rank 的总代价尽可能接近；
    • +
  • 分配完成后，再对每个 rank 内部的 microbatch 顺序做代价对齐，让各 rank 在同一个 microbatch 序号上处理量级相近的样本，避免「同一时刻有的卡在算长样本、有的卡在算短样本」造成的逐 microbatch 抖动。
    • +
+ +

效果同样用端到端耗时验证：开启代价均衡采样后，单步耗时下降 7.4%（提速 1.079 倍）。这是一项不改变任何算子实现、纯靠数据编排拿到的收益，也是纯算子优化拿不到的那部分。

+

需要强调的是，均衡改变了样本到 rank 的映射，因此必须证明它不改变训练语义。我们为此建立了样本顺序的 SHA256 门禁：导出每个 rank 每个 epoch 的实际取样顺序，与归档基线逐文件校验，任何一个文件不一致即判定门禁失败。

+

优化三：逐层算子链融合 —— 手写 Triton RoPE、融合 QK RMSNorm、编译调制前缀

+

30 层 block 中的「小操作」是最容易被忽略的成本。它们单个只有几微秒，但每层都要做、每个 microbatch 都要做，还会在反向中留下一串中间张量。LoongForge 在这一层做了三件事：

+

手写 Triton RoPE 算子。旋转位置编码在 eager 实现下会展开成 mul / add / cat / copy 的算子链，Q 和 K 各走一遍。我们用一个 Triton kernel 同时完成 Q、K 的成对旋转，并自己实现 backward——反向的旋转与正向共享同一段 kernel，只需把旋转方向取反，因此不需要保存额外的中间张量，也不需要在反向中重建算子链；cos/sin 频率分量按形状缓存复用。消融显示，关闭这一组后 elementwise 总时间涨到原来的 1.76 倍，kernel 数增加约 5100 个/step，单步耗时上涨 7.29%；而且其中约 98% 的收益来自 backward——这正是自己写反向的价值所在。

+

融合 QK RMSNorm。Q/K 归一化如果走框架原生实现，会在注意力前后产生额外的 contiguous 拷贝与 dtype 转换。我们改用 TransformerEngine 的融合 RMSNorm，消融实验中关闭该项优化会导致端到端单步耗时上涨 6.46%，证明了该项优化的有效性。

+

编译逐层调制前缀并固定 BF16 计算域。每层的时间调制（shift / scale / gate）叠加 LayerNorm 是一段典型的「访存受限的短链」。我们把它整体作为一个编译单元，让编译器在一个 kernel 内完成调制与归一化，并把 block 内的中间表达式统一保持在 BF16、不做来回升降精度。关闭调制前缀编译后单步耗时上涨 7.78%，elementwise 总时间涨到原来的 1.9 倍；固定 BF16 计算域这一项另有约 1.4% 的收益。

+ +

优化四：把 GPU 从「等主机」里救出来 —— 掩码编译、GC 抑制

+

前三项都在减少 GPU 要做的工作。但 profiling 还暴露了另一类浪费：GPU 明明有活可干，却在空转等主机。

+

判读依据是 NSys 的三个结构指标：GPU busy 占比、GPU idle 时间、以及 kernel 之间「≥10 微秒的可见空隙」总时长。如果一项改动使 kernel 数量、各类别 kernel 时间几乎不变，但 idle 与大空隙同步显著上涨，那它就是一个主机侧瓶颈——这类瓶颈无法靠优化算子解决，只能把主机侧计算移出关键路径。

+ +

沿着这个判据，我们主要定位并解决了两类主机侧瓶颈：

+
    +
  • 注意力掩码构造。交织序列的稀疏注意力需要逐 step 构造 block mask，这是 Python 侧的图结构计算。未编译时，它直接阻塞 forward 的 kernel 提交：GPU busy 从 99.0% 掉到 94.8%，GPU idle 涨到原来的 5.6 倍，≥10 微秒空隙涨到原来的 10.4 倍——而且idle 的增量与大空隙的增量几乎逐毫秒相等，是 GPU 等 host 的教科书特征。我们对掩码构造做编译并按形状/窗口参数缓存复用（编译失败自动回退 eager，保证鲁棒性），把这段主机计算从关键路径上摘掉，单步收益 3.89%。
    • +
  • Python 自动垃圾回收。训练主循环会产生大量短生命周期对象，Python 的 generation-2 full GC 一旦触发，主机侧会出现一段无法提交 CUDA 工作的空窗；更糟的是各 rank 的触发时刻不一致，空窗会通过集合通信被放大。我们的策略不是简单关掉 GC，而是保留 generation-0/1 的年轻代回收、把 generation-2 阈值抑制掉，并在固定 step 间隔显式触发一次可控的 full GC。消融显示：回退该策略后 kernel 数完全不变（逐个相同），但 GPU idle 涨到原来的 2.4 倍，单步耗时上涨 1.98%——GPU 计算图一模一样，损失纯粹来自主机停顿。
    • +
+

4. 性能实测

+

在百度百舸平台 hpas.lgn7ib 实例上、使用 LIBERO 数据集对 LingBot-VA 进行默认训练参数测试（gradient accumulation = 10）。在模型结构、数据、超参完全一致的前提下，LoongForge 相对社区开源实现取得 2.20 倍的训练吞吐提升，单步训练耗时缩短 54.5%，同时训练 loss 与社区实现保持对齐（平均相对误差 0.171%）。

+ +

从优化机制看，各方向的贡献量级也很清晰：

+
    +
  • 通信次数放大是唯一能造成 20% 以上单项收益的机制，且收益随梯度累积步数线性放大；
    • +
  • 逐层算子链融合（调制前缀、Triton RoPE、融合 QK RMSNorm）每项对应 6%–8%；
    • +
  • 变长样本的代价均衡采样贡献约 8%，且完全不依赖算子改动；
    • +
  • 主机侧空转治理（掩码编译、GC 策略）合计约 6%，把 GPU busy 推到 99.0%。
    • +
+

值得一提的是，当 GPU busy 达到 99.0% 后，主机侧可挖的空间已不足 1%——后续的提速空间必须回到 kernel 本身（当前 GEMM 约占 kernel 时间的 63.7%）与通信重叠上。这也是我们下一阶段的工作方向。

+

5. 总结：把 GPU 从「被动等待」变成「持续计算」

+

回顾整个优化过程，2.20 倍的提升来自四条不同性质的路径：通信语义的重新设计（参数在 step 内复用）、数据编排的负载均衡（变长样本的代价对齐）、算子层面的手写与融合（Triton RoPE 与逐层链融合）、以及主机侧关键路径的清理（掩码编译、GC 策略）。它们分别对应通信、负载、计算与调度四类浪费，缺一项都拿不到完整收益。

+

支撑这些判断的，是一套「先量化瓶颈、再设计优化、最后消融验收」的方法论：所有结论都来自可复现的时间线证据与逐项消融，所有性能收益都通过与社区实现逐 iteration 对齐的精度门禁。

+

目前，相关优化已全部集成至全模态训练框架 LoongForge。我们欢迎具身智能领域的研究者与开发者一起探索更高效的 VLA 训练方案。

How to Speed Up VLA Training Step by Step: A 3x Acceleration Case Study on Pi0.5

+
2026-10-19 · The LoongForge Team
+
+ +
+
+
GitHubhttps://github.com/baidu-baige/LoongForge
+
Original post (Zhihu)https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2095555587304117777
+
+

We recently finished accelerating Pi0.5 SFT training on LoongForge.

+

Before we started, we figured a 3.5B model with a 762-token sequence would not need many tricks. In practice, there turned out to be a lot to refine.

+

The end result: 24.0 samples/s in bf16 (2.63x the community implementation) and 27.34 samples/s in FP8 (3.00x).

+

1. A redundant 256 tokens: pruning the empty camera slot

+

The Pi0.5 sequence has an unusual structure made of three parts: images, a text instruction, and actions. To separate the compute load of the ViT from that of the backbone attention, we first broke the sequence length down by branch.

+

For the two-camera LIBERO data, the joint sequence of images (2×256), instruction and actions (50) should be 762 tokens. The length we actually saw while debugging was 1018, i.e. 256 tokens of pure padding.

+

The cause: openpi's Pi0.5 input has three fixed camera slots. When only two cameras are present, the missing one is filled with a placeholder image and its image mask is set to False.

+

But that mask only makes those 256 tokens invisible to attention; none of the computation is actually skipped. The placeholder image still goes through SigLIP, its 256 tokens still run through all 18 decoder layers, and their activations are still saved, even though no valid token attends to them and they take no part in the loss.

+ +

So LoongForge allocates slots on demand on the data side (set data.num_images to the actual number of cameras) and creates slots only for cameras that exist. Pad tokens do not advance position_ids. After pruning, the positional encoding and visibility of the valid tokens are unchanged and the loss is strictly identical, yet roughly 25% of the compute and the corresponding activation memory are saved.

+

2. Dense, fragmented small ops: accelerating with torch.compile

+

Profiling shows that apart from a few large GEMMs, each Pi0.5 layer is made of small operators (especially in the action expert, which has a small hidden size): adaRMS normalization, RoPE, concatenating and splitting Q/K/V across the two branches, gelu·up, and gated residuals.

+

In eager mode, every small op launches its own kernel and keeps its intermediate result in memory. Take adaRMS: cast to fp32, square, mean, rsqrt, chunk out scale/shift/gate, cast back to bf16. Each step produces a full-size intermediate tensor.

+

That makes torch.compile an obvious candidate. But Pi0.5 is quite dynamic, so the whole model cannot simply be compiled:

+
    +
  • The vision tower is dynamic and follows the number of images. + embed_prefix runs SigLIP on each image in a Python for loop whose trip count depends on the dataset's camera count. The per-image pad mask and block-start markers are also assembled in Python according to the image count and moved to the GPU with torch.tensor. Compiling this directly easily causes graph breaks or recompiles.
    • +
  • The ViT is not a large share of the time, so compiling it pays off less. Running two images through SigLIP takes only about 20% of the forward pass; the 18 decoder layers take nearly 80%.
    • +
+

So we keep the vision tower and prefix assembly in eager mode and compile only the fixed-shape backbone (paligemma_with_expert). With torch.compile on, Inductor performs three main kinds of fusion:

+
    +
  • Elementwise + reduction fused into one kernel: the whole adaRMS chain becomes a single persistent reduction kernel, with the mean and rsqrt computed in one pass; the residual add and post_attention_layernorm are fused as well.
    • +
  • Small ops fused into the GEMM: the adaRMS modulation and dtype conversion are absorbed into the Triton GEMM of q_proj, so the normalized result does not need a separate round trip through memory.
    • +
  • RoPE collapsed end to end: building the cos/sin tables (broadcast multiply, cat, cos/sin, cast) becomes one kernel, and q * cos + rotate_half(q) * sin becomes another, which can run at the memory-bandwidth limit.
    • +
+

With this partial compilation, training throughput improved by 54%.

+

3. An unexpected memory win: FlexAttention to shrink activations

+

Coming from an LLM mindset, we first looked at the attention part of Pi0.5. Profiling showed that, unlike a typical LLM, attention does not account for much of the end-to-end time: with a sequence of only 762 tokens, attention is about 13% of a decoder layer, while the MLP takes about 76%. End to end, the attention forward pass is only about 2.8%, so there is very little compute time to win back.

+

What profiling did reveal is that attention produces many activations and many fragmented ops. The eager implementation first uses repeat_kv to copy the single KV head into 8, then materializes the full [B, 8, T, T] probability matrix. Scaling, mask addition, the two-pass softmax, PV and the transpose back are each a separate kernel; every intermediate result has to be kept for the backward pass, and softmax additionally stores an fp32 copy. Even under torch.compile, the activation cost did not drop noticeably.

+

On the other hand, the Pi0.5 mask is naturally suited to block-sparse attention:

+
    +
  • The prefix (images + text) is fully bidirectional internally but cannot see the actions, so the whole upper-right block is masked out;
    • +
  • Actions can see every valid prefix token, and the 50 action tokens can see each other;
    • +
  • Rows and columns that correspond to padding are masked out entirely.
    • +
+ +

Large regions of the mask are either fully visible or fully masked, which fits FlexAttention's BlockMask: the mask is described in 128×128 tiles, fully masked tiles are skipped outright, and only tiles on the boundary are evaluated element by element.

+ +

After switching to FlexAttention, enable_gqa=True broadcasts the KV head inside the kernel instead of copying it, and the backward pass stores only the output and the logsumexp. Speed is about the same as eager (±2%) and makes little difference end to end, but at a micro batch size of 32 each layer stores about 0.63 GiB less, roughly 11 GiB across 18 layers.

+

4. Selective recomputation

+

openpi enables full recomputation by default: activations of the vision tower, the 18 decoder layers, the embeddings and the action/time projections are never stored, and the whole forward pass is recomputed during backward.

+

On LoongForge, with torch.compile and FlexAttention stacked on top, activation memory already drops considerably, but matching the official batch size still requires recomputation.

+

The question becomes: which part is the best one to recompute? We measured the cost-effectiveness of recomputing each module (the extra milliseconds spent per GiB of activations saved):

+
    +
  • ViT (27 SigLIP layers): 2.8 ms/GiB, +48.5 ms to save 17.5 GiB. The ViT hidden size is narrow (1152 vs. 2048 for Gemma), so the same FLOPs produce the most activations, which makes recomputing it the cheapest.
    • +
  • PaliGemma MLP: 4.0 ms/GiB. It has the largest activations (37.6 GiB), but costs +150 ms.
    • +
  • Attention (norm + QKV + RoPE + FlexAttention): 7.8 ms/GiB, storing only 5.5 GiB over 18 layers. MQA's K/V are small and FlexAttention does not store a score matrix, yet recomputing means running the QKV projection and the attention forward again. Small activations and expensive compute make it the worst deal.
    • +
  • Gemma Expert MLP: it processes only 50 action tokens and totals 0.7 GiB across 18 layers, so recomputing it or not is within the noise.
    • +
+

We therefore chose to recompute only the ViT (using LoongForge's --activation-checkpoint-module-patterns to match only the SigLIP layers), which keeps the recomputation overhead as low as possible.

+

5. The communication bottleneck without NVLink: layered compilation to hide the gradient AllReduce

+

With NVLink, gradient communication is usually not a bottleneck. In our actual training setup, however, PCIe communication is expensive: the bf16 gradients of Pi0.5's 3.5B parameters are about 7 GB, and a ring AllReduce moves 12.25 GB per GPU, taking as much as 220 ms.

+

Profiling showed that because the whole backbone was initially compiled by torch.compile into a single graph, the backward Inductor generates is one monolithic autograd Function. All parameter gradients therefore become ready only at the very end of the backward pass, so the DDP gradient buckets can only run serially after backward, and about 215 ms of communication per step is fully exposed.

+

5.1 The intended use of DDPOptimizer + torch.compile: wrap the whole model and schedule it together with communication

+

PyTorch ran into this problem long ago. The core idea is: the larger the scope the compiler sees, the better. Ideally you hand it the whole model, or even a whole training step, and it schedules gradient communication and overlaps it with compute.

+
    +
  • DDPOptimizer (on by default since PyTorch 2.0): when torch.compile is applied to a DDP-wrapped model, Dynamo splits the forward graph along DDP bucket boundaries and compiles each piece separately, so backward gradients become ready in batches.
    • +
+

Its precondition, however, is that the model can be captured as a single full graph.

+

5.2 Partial compilation is incompatible with DDPOptimizer

+

As noted above, the peculiar ViT structure of Pi0.5 prevents compiling the whole model with torch.compile. Compiling only the backbone means explicitly calling torch.compile on a submodule inside DDP, and then DDPOptimizer crashes:

+
    +
  • Symptom: the first launch after clearing the compile cache always fails with BackendCompilerFailed, ultimately caused by accessing data_ptr() on a FakeTensor; restarting without clearing the cache works. This was very misleading, and we suspected autotune or CUDA Graphs for a while.
    • +
  • Root cause: +
      +
    • DDPOptimizer wraps another layer of compilation on the outside, producing nested compilation. Before compiling the next subgraph, DDPOptimizer runs the previously compiled subgraph under FakeTensorMode to obtain the output shape/stride. The AOTAutograd runtime wrapper of the inner compile does not know it is in FakeTensorMode, takes the real autograd.Function.apply path, and fails on the FakeTensor's data_ptr().
      • +
    • A warm cache works only because an FX graph cache hit bypasses this path. Changing the shape, the number of ranks, or clearing the cache reproduces the failure.
      • +
    +
    • +
+

So we had to turn it off first (--no-dynamo-optimize-ddp). The cost is exactly what we analyzed above: with nobody splitting the graph, gradients only become ready after the entire backward graph finishes, and the communication is completely exposed.

+

5.3 Layered compilation: splitting the graph by hand

+

Since a full-graph compile is not possible and DDPOptimizer cannot be used, we simply split the graph ourselves inside the backbone.

+

We switched the compilation strategy to multi_group compilation: each of the 18 decoder layers is its own compilation unit (identical shapes are compiled once and the other 17 layers reuse the result), and the final norm, the action input projection + time MLP, and the action output projection each become their own small graph.

+

As a result, the backward of every layer is an independent autograd.Function: as soon as the backward of layer N finishes, its gradient bucket can launch AllReduce immediately, overlapping with the backward compute of layer N-1.

+

In essence, this implements by hand what DDPOptimizer is meant to do, only with the split points pinned exactly to layer boundaries, and with no dependency on DDPOptimizer at all. With manual layered compilation the exposed communication essentially disappears, for a +10% throughput gain.

+

6. Validating bf16 quality: the LIBERO evaluation

+

With the bf16 optimizations above combined, end-to-end training throughput rises to 24.0 samples/s, 2.63x the community throughput.

+

For quality, the LoongForge bf16 model's 5-run average results on the four LIBERO suites are:

+

7. Pushing compute further with FP8

+

By this point, there is little left to squeeze out of bf16. Next we moved all Linear modules in Pi0.5 to FP8 compute: inputs and weights are quantized to FP8 for the GEMM, the result is restored using the scales, and the tensors stay in bf16 before and after the computation.

+

7.1 Trying FP8 with TransformerEngine

+

The first thing we tried was TransformerEngine's FP8: replace nn.Linear with te.Linear and wrap the forward pass in fp8_autocast. The real problem is that it conflicts with the earlier optimizations:

+
    +
  • It conflicts with torch.compile and breaks the graph everywhere. +
      +
    • TE has internal functions decorated with @torch.compiler.disable() (fp8 metadata and amax handling).
      • +
    • Dynamo therefore breaks the graph at every te.Linear: 218 Linear layers mean more than 200 graph breaks, and the adaRMS and gelu·up fusions before and after each Linear can no longer attach to the GEMM.
      • +
    +
    • +
  • Graph breaks directly raise activation memory. +
      +
    • With a full graph, AOTAutograd partitions forward and backward together, so cheap elementwise ops such as adaRMS, gelu·up, RoPE and residuals are recomputed in backward and only a few tensors are saved.
      • +
    • After graph breaks, a layer is cut into several segments: the Linear input must actually be written to memory, the Linear stores another copy for backward, and nothing can be recomputed across segments. Accumulated over 18 layers this adds about 13 GiB.
      • +
    +
    • +
+

So TE's FP8 GEMM itself is fine, but inside the torch.compile-centered optimization path of Pi0.5, the graph breaks and the extra memory eat up the gains and easily turn them negative.

+

7.2 FP8 with TorchAO

+

TE's problem is graph breaks, so we looked for an FP8 solution that can stay inside the compiled graph. That led us to TorchAO with the tensorwise recipe.

+

In TorchAO's Float8Linear, amax, scale and cast are all ordinary PyTorch ops and the GEMM goes through torch._scaled_mm, so Dynamo can trace it directly into a graph.

+

In measurements, memory use was actually lower than bf16. Our hypothesis: the Float8Linear autograd Function is written to save the bf16 input for backward, but because it lives inside the compiled graph, the partitioner can see that backward only re-casts this input to FP8 to compute wgrad, so it stores the FP8 version plus one scale instead, which halves these activations.

+

Which Linear layers use TorchAO FP8 is decided in two stages:

+
    +
  • Static rules: +
      +
    • Of 458 candidates, precision-sensitive modules (vision_tower, multi_modal_projector, the action/time projections) keep their original precision, skipping 204;
      • +
    • another 36 small Linear layers are dropped via fp8-min-dim=2048, because their GEMMs are so small that the quantization overhead exceeds the time FP8 saves.
      • +
    +
    • +
  • Trace validation: +
      +
    • We use Kineto traces to map every GEMM back to its module by shape, compare measured bf16 and FP8 kernel times, and keep only the ones that actually get faster;
      • +
    • The PaliGemma MLP and the attention projections are both 1.8–2.0x faster; two lm_head layers that never execute during training are excluded, leaving 216 in the end.
      • +
    +
    • +
+

In the end, GEMM's share of a step falls from 54% to 33%, and throughput improves by another 13.9% on top of bf16, reaching 27.34 samples/s, 3.0x the community implementation.

+

On accuracy, compared with bf16 the loss has a Pearson correlation of 0.9997 and a mean relative error of 0.56%.

最近我们在 LoongForge 上完成了 Pi0.5 的 SFT 加速训练。

+

优化开始之前，原本认为：3.5B 的模型、762 的序列长度，看上去用不了多少 trick。但实际优化下来，发现可以细化的地方很多。

+

最终 bf16 下吞吐做到 24.0 samples/s（社区实现的 2.63 倍），FP8 下吞吐达到 27.34 samples/s（社区实现的 3.00 倍）。

+

1. 冗余的 256 序列长度：空相机 slot 裁剪

+

Pi0.5 的序列结构比较特殊，包含图像、文本指令和 action 三部分。为了理清 ViT 与主干 Attention 各自的计算负载，优化前先对各分支的序列长度做了分解。

+

按两路相机的 LIBERO 数据推算，图像（2×256）、指令与 action（50）拼起来的联合序列本应是 762，但实际 debug 出来的序列长度却是 1018，平白多出了 256 的无效 padding。

+

排查发现，openpi 的 Pi0.5 输入固定 3 个相机 slot。当输入只有 2 路相机的时候，也会默认给缺的那路填一张占位图，再把 image mask 置为 False。

+

然而这个 mask 只是让这 256 个 token 在注意力里不可见，实际的计算一点没少：占位图依旧需要计算 SigLIP，产出的 256 个 token 也得过 18 层 decoder layer，中间的激活值照样保存，哪怕它们既不会被有效 token 注意到，也不参与最终的 loss 计算。

+ +

因此，LoongForge 在数据侧改为按需分配（将 data.num_images 设为实际相机数），只为真实存在的相机输入生成 slot；对于原本的 pad token，不推进 position_ids。裁剪后有效 token 的位置编码和可见范围不变，loss 与裁剪前严格一致，但直接省去了约 25% 的计算量和相应的激活值显存占用。

+

2. 密集的细碎算子开销：torch.compile 加速

+

通过 profile 发现，Pi0.5 每层除了几颗大 GEMM，剩下全是小算子（尤其是 hidden size 较小的 action expert），包括 adaRMS 归一化、RoPE、两个分支 Q/K/V 的拼接与切回、gelu·up、门控残差。

+

在 eager 模式下，每个小算子都会触发一次独立的 kernel 启动，中间结果常驻显存。以 adaRMS 为例，cast 到 fp32、平方、求均值、rsqrt、chunk 出 scale/shift/gate、cast 回 bf16，每一步都产生一个完整大小的中间张量。

+

因此我们考虑用 torch.compile 加速。但 Pi0.5 是比较动态的模型，不能对整个模型直接 compile：

+
    +
  • vision tower 是动态的，跟着图像数量走。 + embed_prefix 用 for 循环逐张图过 SigLIP，循环次数取决于数据集的相机数；每张图的 pad mask 和块起始标记也是在 Python 里按图像数动态拼好，再通过 torch.tensor 搬到 GPU 上，直接编译极易触发断图或重编。
    • +
  • ViT 的耗时占比没有那么高，编它的收益相对有限。两路图像过 SigLIP 只占前向的 20%，18 层 decoder layer 占近 80%。
    • +
+

因此，我们让 Pi0.5 的 vision tower 和 prefix 拼接部分保持 eager，只局部编译后面形状固定的 backbone（paligemma_with_expert）。开启 torch.compile 之后，Inductor 主要做了三类融合：

+
    +
  • 逐元素 + 归约融成一颗 kernel：adaRMS 整串操作融成一颗 persistent reduction kernel，均值和 rsqrt 单趟算完；残差加和 post_attention_layernorm 也融在一起。
    • +
  • 小算子融进 GEMM：adaRMS 的调制和类型转换被吃进 q_proj 的 Triton GEMM，归一化结果不用单独落一次显存。
    • +
  • RoPE 整段折叠：cos/sin 表的构造（广播乘、cat、cos/sin、cast）融成一颗 kernel，q * cos + rotate_half(q) * sin 融成一颗，可以跑到显存带宽上限。
    • +
+

经过局部编译后，训练吞吐提升了 54%。

+

3. 意外的显存收益：FlexAttention 压激活值

+

从 LLM 的惯性思维出发，我们最开始看的是 Pi0.5 的 Attention 部分。但 profile 发现，与普通的 LLM 不同，Pi0.5 的 attention 在端到端里的耗时占比并不高：序列长度只有 762，attention 计算在 decoder layer 内占比约 13%，剩下主要是 MLP，约占 76%。折到端到端，attention 前向只占约 2.8%，计算耗时的优化空间很小。

+

不过 profile 过程中发现，它的激活值多、算子碎。eager 实现每层先用 repeat_kv 把唯一的 KV 头复制成 8 份，再物化完整的 [B, 8, T, T] 概率矩阵；乘 scale、加 mask、两趟 softmax、PV、transpose 回去，每一步都是独立的 kernel，中间结果反向时都得留着，softmax 还会多存一份 fp32 中间结果。即使在 torch.compile 包裹下，激活值的开销也没有显著降低。

+

另一方面，Pi0.5 的掩码天然适合块稀疏（Block-Sparse）的 attention：

+
    +
  • prefix（图像 + 文本）内部完全双向，但看不到 action，右上角整块屏蔽；
    • +
  • action 能看到全部有效 prefix，50 个 action token 之间也互相可见；
    • +
  • pad 所在的行和列整体屏蔽。
    • +
+ +

掩码里大片区域要么全可见、要么全屏蔽，正好对上 FlexAttention 的 BlockMask：按 128×128 的 tile 描述掩码，整块屏蔽的 tile 直接跳过，只有边界上的 tile 才逐元素判断。

+ +

替换为 FlexAttention 后，enable_gqa=True 让 KV 头在 kernel 内广播，不再复制；反向只存输出和 logsumexp。速度和 eager 差不多（±2%），在端到端上区别不大，但 micro batch size 为 32 时每层少存约 0.63 GiB，18 层合计约 11 GiB。

+

4. 选择性重计算

+

openpi 默认开启全量重计算：视觉塔、18 层 decoder layer、embedding 以及 action/time 投影的激活值一律不存，反向传播时全部重算一遍前向。

+

在 LoongForge 框架下，叠加 torch.compile 和 FlexAttention 之后，激活值显存占用已经大幅度下降，但想要对齐官方的 batch size，还是需要开启重计算。

+

问题就变成了：只重算哪一部分最划算？我们按模块逐个测算了重计算的"性价比"（即每省 1 GiB 激活需要多花多少毫秒）：

+
    +
  • ViT（SigLIP 27 层）：2.8 ms/GiB，+48.5 ms 换 17.5 GiB。ViT 的 hidden 窄（1152 vs Gemma 的 2048），同样的 FLOP 产生的激活最多，重算最便宜。
    • +
  • PaliGemma MLP：4.0 ms/GiB，激活最大（37.6 GiB），但要 +150 ms。
    • +
  • Attention（norm + QKV + RoPE + FlexAttention）：7.8 ms/GiB，18 层只存 5.5 GiB。MQA 的 K/V 很小，FlexAttention 也不存 score 矩阵，可重算要把 QKV 投影和 attention 前向再跑一遍。激活小、算得贵，最不划算。
    • +
  • Gemma Expert MLP：只处理 50 个 action token，18 层合计 0.7 GiB，重不重算都在噪声里。
    • +
+

最终我们选择只重算 ViT（通过 LoongForge 框架的 --activation-checkpoint-module-patterns 仅匹配 SigLIP 层），把重算开销降到了最低。

+

5. 无 NVLink 场景下的通信瓶颈：分层编译隐藏梯度 AllReduce

+

NVLink 场景下梯度通信通常不是瓶颈，但在我们实际训练的场景下，PCIe 通信代价高昂：Pi0.5 的 3.5B 参数的 bf16 梯度约 7 GB，ring AllReduce 每卡需要传输 12.25 GB，通信耗时高达 220 ms。

+

然而 profile 发现，由于一开始把整个 backbone 用 torch.compile 编成一张图，Inductor 生成的反向是一个整体的 autograd Function，这导致所有参数梯度在反向结束时才同时 ready，DDP 梯度桶只能串行排在反向之后，每步有高达约 215 ms 的通信开销完全暴露。

+

5.1 DDPOptimizer + torch.compile 的预期用法：包住整个模型，和通信一起调度

+

这个问题 PyTorch 官方早就遇到过，其核心思路是：编译器看到的范围越大越好——最好将整模型甚至整步训练交给它，由其统一调度梯度通信的时机与计算重叠。

+
    +
  • DDPOptimizer（PyTorch 2.0 起，默认开启）：对 DDP 包住的模型调用 torch.compile 时，Dynamo 会顺着 DDP bucket 的大小将前向图切段分别编译，从而让反向梯度分批就绪。
    • +
+

但它的前提是模型能被完整抓成整图。

+

5.2 局部 compile 与 DDPOptimizer 不兼容

+

前面提到，Pi0.5 特殊的 ViT 结构决定了它无法对整个模型直接 torch.compile；只编 backbone，意味着要在 DDP 内部对子模块显式 torch.compile，这时 DDPOptimizer 会崩：

+
    +
  • 现象：清空编译缓存后第一次启动必挂，报 BackendCompilerFailed，最终是 FakeTensor 上访问了 data_ptr()；不清缓存直接重启又能跑。很有迷惑性，一度以为是 autotune 或 CUDA Graph 的问题。
    • +
  • 根因： +
      +
    • DDPOptimizer 在外面又套了一层，形成嵌套编译。DDPOptimizer 编译下一段子图前，会在 FakeTensorMode 下执行上一段已编译的子图来拿输出的 shape/stride，而里层 compile 的 AOTAutograd runtime wrapper 不知道自己处于 FakeTensorMode，会走真实的 autograd.Function.apply，碰到 FakeTensor 的 data_ptr() 就挂。
      • +
    • 热缓存能跑，只是因为命中 FX graph cache 绕开了这条路径，换个 shape、换个 rank 数或者清一次缓存就会复现。
      • +
    +
    • +
+

所以只能先关掉它（--no-dynamo-optimize-ddp）。代价正如前面所分析的：由于无人帮忙切图，整张反向图跑完后梯度才能 ready，通信完全暴露出去了。

+

5.3 自行分层编译，手动切图

+

既然整图编译无法实现、DDPOptimizer 又无法使用，干脆就在 backbone 内部自己动手切图。

+

我们将编译策略改为 multi_group 分组编译：18 个 decoder layer 各自作为一个独立的编译单元（相同 shape 只需编译一次，其余 17 层直接复用），同时将 final norm、action 输入投影 + time MLP、action 输出投影各自独立成小图。

+

这样一来，每一层的反向都成为了独立的 autograd.Function：当第 N 层的反向一结束，它的梯度桶就能立刻发起 AllReduce，与第 N-1 层的反向计算并行重叠。

+

本质上，这相当于手动实现了 DDPOptimizer 想做的事，只是将切分点精准锁在了层边界上，完全摆脱了对 DDPOptimizer 的依赖。改用手动分层编译后，暴露的通信基本消失，吞吐 +10%。

+

+

7. 极致 FP8 计算优化

+

到这里，bf16 下能抠的性能基本已经见底。接下来，我们将 Pi0.5 中的 Linear 模块全面推进到 FP8 计算：输入与权重量化为 FP8 后执行 GEMM，结果按 scale 还原，计算前后保持 bf16。

+

7.1 TransformerEngine 的 FP8 尝试

+

最先尝试的是 TransformerEngine 的 FP8 方案：把 nn.Linear 换成 te.Linear，前向套上 fp8_autocast。但真正的问题是它和前面的优化冲突：

+
    +
  • 和 torch.compile 冲突，到处断图。 +
      +
    • TE 内部有被 @torch.compiler.disable() 装饰的函数（fp8 元数据和 amax 处理）。
      • +
    • Dynamo 于是在每个 te.Linear 处断图，218 个 Linear 就是 200 多处断图，Linear 前后的 adaRMS、gelu·up 这些融合也接不到 GEMM 上了。
      • +
    +
    • +
  • 断图直接推高激活值显存占用。 +
      +
    • 整图时 AOTAutograd 把前向和反向放在一起切分，adaRMS、gelu·up、RoPE、残差这类便宜的逐元素算子会留到反向重算，只存少量张量。
      • +
    • 断图之后一层被切成好几段，Linear 的输入必须真实写到显存里，Linear 自己再为反向存一份，前后两段之间也没法跨段重算。18 层累加下来多了约 13 GiB。
      • +
    +
    • +
+

所以 TE 的 FP8 GEMM 本身没问题，但放进 Pi0.5 这条以 torch.compile 为核心的优化路径里，断图和多出来的显存把收益吃掉了，很容易导出负收益。

+

7.2 TorchAO 的 FP8 方案

+

TE 的问题在于断图，那就找一个能留在编译图里的 FP8 方案。于是我们考虑 TorchAO，使用 tensorwise recipe。

+

TorchAO 的 Float8Linear 的 amax、scale、cast 都是普通的 PyTorch 算子，GEMM 走 torch._scaled_mm，在 Dynamo 下能直接建图。

+

实测显存反而比 bf16 更省。我们推测原因是：Float8Linear 的 autograd Function 本身写的是为反向保存 bf16 输入，但它在编译图里，partitioner 看得到反向拿这份输入只是重新 cast 成 FP8 再算 wgrad，于是改为直接存 FP8 版本加一个 scale，这部分激活减半。

+

至于哪些 Linear 走 TorchAO FP8，分两层筛选：

+
    +
  • 静态规则： +
      +
    • 458 个候选里，精度敏感的模块（vision_tower、multi_modal_projector、action/time 投影）保留原精度，跳过 204 个；
      • +
    • 再按 fp8-min-dim=2048 去掉 36 个小 Linear，它们的 GEMM 太小，量化开销比 FP8 省下的时间还多。
      • +
    +
    • +
  • trace 验证： +
      +
    • 用 Kineto trace 把每个 GEMM 按 shape 归回模块，对比 bf16 与 FP8 的实测 kernel 耗时，只留确实变快的；
      • +
    • PaliGemma MLP 和 attention 投影都快了 1.8–2.0 倍；2 个训练中不会执行的 lm_head 被排除，最终保留 216 个。
      • +
    +
    • +
+

最终 GEMM 在单步中的占比从 54% 降到 33%，吞吐在 bf16 的基础上再提升 13.9%，做到 27.34 samples/s，是社区实现的 3.0 倍。

+

精度上，与 bf16 对比，loss 的 Pearson 相关系数为 0.9997，平均相对误差 0.56%。
